title: The Dragonfly's Eye: My Virtual Camera (AI)
description:
A late book by the German filmmaker and writer Alexander Kluge that takes AI image generation as a new kind of camera and asks what its pictures can and cannot show.

Kluge looks at the quirks of these images, where chance and error produce what the publisher calls subjunctive forms: open images that are hard to place. The 480-page pocket-format hardcover builds its stories around them, moving between cases as unlike as East German phantom pregnancies and present-day political figures. The AI works as a virtual camera that tells and re-imagines space through pictures. Spector Books issued it in 2024, with a separate German edition titled Der Konjunktiv der Bilder.

Kluge was born in Halberstadt in 1932 and died in 2026. He signed the 1962 Oberhausen Manifesto and became a leading figure of New German Cinema, with Yesterday Girl (1966) winning a Silver Lion at Venice. From 1987 he produced television through his company dctp, and he wrote theory with Oskar Negt, including Public Sphere and Experience and History and Obstinacy. He received the Georg Büchner Prize in 2003.

title: Goodbye, World! Looking at Art in the Digital Age
description:
A curator's argument that art made and seen in a networked world has to be looked at differently.

Sternberg Press published the 212-page paperback in 2018. Kholeif asks how life and art have changed in the twenty-first century. He treats the internet as a replacement for older ways of picturing the world. John Berger's Ways of Seeing and Alvin Toffler's Future Shock are his stated inspirations. The text mixes memoir with critical analysis of image perception, technology and post-digital practice. It has 195 colour illustrations and was designed by Zak Group.

Kholeif is an Egyptian-born curator and writer. He has worked at the Whitechapel Gallery, HOME Manchester and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, and later directed collections at the Sharjah Art Foundation. The book follows You Are Here: Art After the Internet (2014). Art in the Age of Anxiety (2021) and Internet_Art (2023) came after it.

title: antiDATA: la désobéissance numérique. Art et hacktivisme technocritique
description:
A French-language study of artists, hackers and activists who answer the power of digital platforms with acts of disobedience.

Les presses du réel published the 232-page paperback in November 2020 in its Perceptions collection, with 51 colour illustrations. Fourmentraux examines resistance to the dominance of technological innovation through counter-surveillance, tactical media, speculative design and data visualization. Trevor Paglen, Paolo Cirio and Julien Prévieux are among the artists discussed. The book argues that these practices challenge the sovereignty of platforms while writing the histories of code and cryptography into cultural critique.

Fourmentraux holds a doctorate in socio-anthropology and is a professor at Aix-Marseille University. He is an art critic affiliated with AICA and a member of the Centre Norbert Elias. His earlier books on digital culture include Art et Internet (2005) and L'Ère post-média (2012).

A standard survey of digital art from the 1980s onward, in the compact World of Art series, by a curator of new media.

The third edition, revised and expanded, appeared from Thames & Hudson in 2015 as a 272-page paperback with 338 illustrations. The book also looks at how digital techniques have affected older art forms, and treats internet art, software art, digital installation and virtual reality as established practices.

The book is a general history of the field, written for students and readers new to it. Earlier editions exist: the second edition carries ISBN 9780500203989.

title: Entangled Realities: Living with Artificial Intelligence / Leben mit künstlicher Intelligenz
contributors: Felix Stalder (Essay); Matteo Pasquinelli (Essay); Nora N. Khan (Essay)
description:
The catalogue of a 2019 HeK Basel exhibition on how artificial intelligence shapes the world it claims to describe.

The 224-page volume pairs works by artists including James Bridle, Mario Klingemann, Trevor Paglen and Lauren McCarthy with theoretical texts. Felix Stalder writes on the opacity of machine-learning systems. Matteo Pasquinelli traces the history of the algorithm from ancient Indian rituals to the present. Nora N. Khan contributes a dialogue on machine violence. The editors' own essays document the curatorial process and set out the scientific and artistic context of the show.

Sabine Himmelsbach and Boris Magrini edited the book for HeK. The exhibition treated AI as an immature technology that already fires the public imagination, as virtual reality did in the 1990s. Pasquinelli's contribution links the book to his later The Eye of the Master.

title: The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence
description:
A history of artificial intelligence that locates its origin in the organisation of labour rather than in the imitation of the human brain.

Pasquinelli argues that the logic of AI comes from the automation of work and from the social relations of the factory, including the surveillance of collective behaviour. The 272-page book follows that line from Babbage's calculating engines and the mechanisation of mental labour through Marx's general intellect, Hayek's epistemology of connectionism and the invention of the perceptron, to current image-recognition systems. It rejects the idea that algorithms could become autonomous.

Matteo Pasquinelli is an associate professor of philosophy of science at Ca' Foscari University in Venice. The Eye of the Master was published by Verso in October 2023 and won the 2024 Deutscher Memorial Prize. His essay on the history of the algorithm also appears in the HeK Basel catalogue Entangled Realities.

title: You Are Here: Art After the Internet
description:
An anthology on how the internet changed the making of art, published as the first major book on what was then called post-internet practice.

The book grew out of the SPACE Art + Technology Programme, a yearlong residency at The White Building in London. It gathers essays and artist projects by about twenty-two contributors, among them James Bridle, Jon Rafman, Zach Blas, Erika Balsom, Sophia Al-Maria and Jennifer Chan, with a foreword by Ed Halter. Artist contributions include work by James Richards, Jamie Shovlin, Jeremy Bailey and Jon Rafman. Writers and artists give first-person accounts of working with and through the internet from the early 2000s onward.

Omar Kholeif curated the 2013 programme at The White Building and edited the volume. It was co-published by Cornerhouse and SPACE in spring 2014, with a cover designed by Sam Ashby. SPACE reports three reprints since publication.

description:
The catalogue of a 2016 exhibition at Haus der Kulturen der Welt in Berlin, which asks how sensors and data infrastructures bind state, industry and body into systems that register every tremor of power.

The 388-page English-language volume sets contemporary art beside essays, research and historical documents. It examines how big data and digital infrastructure shape governance and social behaviour, and where "the social question" of power and participation surfaces. Contributors include Grégoire Chamayou, Avery F. Gordon, Orit Halpern, Ben Hayes, Tung-Hui Hu, Lawrence Liang, Noortje Marres, Matteo Pasquinelli, Nishant Shah and Mushon Zer-Aviv. Joris and Terry Kritis designed the small, softcover book.

Anselm Franke edited it for HKW with Stephanie Hankey and Marek Tuszynski, who are from the Tactical Technology Collective. Spector Books published it in Leipzig in April 2016. Pasquinelli, who writes here, later published The Eye of the Master.

title: The AI Mirror: How to Reclaim Our Humanity in an Age of Machine Thinking
description:
A philosophical case that today's AI systems reflect human data and habits back at us, and that mistaking the reflection for a mind distorts how we build and use them.

Vallor builds the book on the mirror metaphor. AI reflects individuals and societies, reproduces existing inequalities, and shows a flattering image of its own benefits. She opens with the case of Blake Lemoine, the Google engineer who took the LaMDA chatbot to be sentient, and argues he was in effect talking to himself. She traces the misconceptions behind this to classical philosophy, including Plato's separation of the technician from society and Aristotle's exclusion of care-work from virtue, and argues for designing technology around human flourishing, care and moral education. Oxford University Press published the hardcover in 2024.

Shannon Vallor is Baillie Gifford Professor in the Ethics of Data and Artificial Intelligence at the University of Edinburgh. Her earlier book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting (2018), applied virtue ethics to technology, drawing on Confucian and Buddhist as well as Western traditions.

title: Video/Art: The First Fifty Years
description:
A history of video art's first five decades by the curator who built the medium's collection and exhibition program at the Museum of Modern Art.

London follows artists as they took up consumer electronics, from analog television monitors to digital projection. Video moved from fringe experiment to a mainstream part of contemporary media art. The book combines art-historical analysis with personal memoir and profiles artists including Joan Jonas, Nam June Paik, Bill Viola, Shirin Neshat, Pipilotti Rist, Miranda July, Ragnar Kjartansson and Ian Cheng. Phaidon published it in 2020, and ARTnews placed it among its best art books of that year.

Barbara London worked at MoMA from 1970 to 2013. She founded its video exhibition and collection programs in the mid-1970s and organized more than 500 media art exhibitions, among them Video Spaces: Eight Installations (1995) and Soundings: A Contemporary Score (2013). She launched the early museum website Stir-Fry in 1997 to document Chinese media art, and now teaches at Yale School of Art. This book draws on that curatorial career.

title: The Synthetic Eye: Photography Transformed in the Age of AI
description:
A critic's survey of what generative AI does to photography, from the trust we place in images to the work photographers can still do with them.

The book asks how we can believe the images we are shown, what duty photographers, media and technology companies have to the authenticity of photographs, and whether synthetic imagery can improve our understanding of the world. It has seven chapters, including a portfolio of synthetic images (Synthetic Dreams) and sections on witnessing, alternative photographies, authorship, and peace and healing. It carries 88 illustrations. Thames & Hudson published it in 2025 in paperback.

Fred Ritchin is Dean Emeritus of the International Center of Photography School and a former professor at NYU Tisch. He was picture editor of The New York Times Magazine from 1978 to 1982 and created the first multimedia version of the newspaper in 1994-95. His earlier books include In Our Own Image, After Photography and Bending the Frame.

title: Atlas of Anomalous AI
description:
An atlas-format anthology that approaches artificial intelligence through art, philosophy and fiction instead of engineering.

The book takes its method from Aby Warburg's Mnemosyne Atlas, an image map of the afterlife of antiquity, and assembles texts, artworks and historical material into a loose constellation. It has three sections, Models, Prediction and Mind, which follow three historical approaches to AI: Symbolic AI, Connectionism and Deep Learning. Contributors include Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Benjamin H. Bratton, Yuk Hui, Nora N. Khan, Hito Steyerl, Jorge Luis Borges, Ian Cheng, Hilma af Klint, Pierre Huyghe and the language models GPT-2 and GPT-3. Some images appear without captions, with explanations gathered at the back of the book. Bill Sherman wrote the foreword. Ignota Books published it in 2020.

Ben Vickers is chief technology officer at the Serpentine Galleries in London and co-founder of Ignota Books. K Allado-McDowell founded the Artists + Machine Intelligence program at Google AI.

title: Curating Digital Art: From Presenting and Collecting Digital Art to Networked Co-Curation
contributors: Marialaura Ghidini (Contributor); Domenico Quaranta (Contributor); Katrina Sluis (Contributor); Constant Dullaart (Contributor); LaTurbo Avedon (Contributor); Katja Novitskova (Contributor); Ryder Ripps (Contributor); Anika Meier (Contributor)
description:
A collection of essays and interviews on how digital and net-based art is shown, collected and kept, edited by the researcher and curator Annet Dekker.

The book asks whether the traditional models and methods of presenting and accessing digital art can be reconfigured. It gathers contributions from curators, artists and researchers on web-based curatorial practice, and on how that practice strains the values of the museum. The title names the arc: from presenting and collecting digital art to what Dekker calls networked co-curation, where the work of selection is shared across a network. It runs to 352 pages in paperback and appeared in Valiz's Making Public series in 2021.

Dekker teaches at the University of Amsterdam and co-directs the Centre for the Study of the Networked Image at London South Bank University. Earlier she was a curator at the Netherlands Media Art Institute and a digital-preservation researcher at Tate. Her monograph Collecting and Conserving Net Art (Routledge, 2018) covers related ground from the conservation side.

title: Art in the Age of Anxiety
contributors: Douglas Coupland (Contributor); Cory Arcangel (Contributor); Simon Denny (Contributor); Heather Dewey-Hagborg (Contributor); W. J. T. Mitchell (Contributor); Hoor Al Qasimi (Contributor)
description:
The reader published for Sharjah Art Foundation's 2020 exhibition of the same name, an edited volume on how networked technology has changed perception, decision-making and mental life.

The exhibition was postponed from March by the pandemic and ran from 26 June to 26 September 2020. It showed more than 60 works by over 30 artists and collectives. The media ranged from sculpture and prints to virtual reality and robotics. The book is a reader more than a catalogue. Its essays cover post-COVID art-making, mental health online, image culture, cryptocurrency and online grieving. Contributors include Douglas Coupland, Cory Arcangel, Simon Denny, Heather Dewey-Hagborg and W. J. T. Mitchell, and Hoor Al Qasimi wrote the foreword. Mörel Books co-published it and MIT Press distributes it.

Omar Kholeif is a curator and writer. He became Director of Collections and Senior Curator at Sharjah Art Foundation in 2019, after posts at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago and Whitechapel Gallery. His earlier books include Goodbye, World! Looking at Art in the Digital Age (Sternberg Press, 2018) and the anthology You Are Here: Art After the Internet.

A handbook on the history of NFTs in art, published for what the Francisco Carolinum in Linz billed as the first museum exhibition on the subject.

The exhibition ran from 10 June to 15 September 2021 and was curated by Jesse Damiani. It showed work by about 25 artists in the museum and in the blockchain-based virtual world Cryptovoxels. The book does not work as a conventional catalogue. It places NFTs in their art-historical context, from the media art of the 1950s and 1960s to contemporary positions. Alfred Weidinger edited the volume for OÖ Landes-Kultur GmbH, the cultural body behind the Linz museum, and wrote its preface. Damiani contributed the introduction. The artists represented include Ai Weiwei, Nam June Paik and Lynn Hershman Leeson. It is a hardcover with a dust jacket and runs to 256 pages.

title: AI: More Than Human

description:
The catalogue to the Barbican's 2019 survey of artificial intelligence, which set the history of AI beside work by artists and research labs.

AI: More than Human ran at the Barbican Centre in London from 16 May to 26 August 2019. It was conceived and curated by Barbican International Enterprises, co-produced with Groninger Forum, and shown as part of the season Life Rewired. The exhibition traced the idea of artificial intelligence from Japanese Shinto animism and the golem legend through Ada Lovelace and Charles Babbage to AlphaGo. It also presented commissions and projects by artists and researchers including Memo Akten, Joy Buolamwini, Stephanie Dinkins, Mario Klingemann, Anna Ridler and teamLab. The book runs to 235 pages.

Chloe Wood, Suzanne Livingston and Maholo Uchida are credited as its editors. Barbican International Enterprises produced both the show and the book.

title: Real Feelings: Emotion and Technology
contributors: Ariane Koek (Essay); António Damásio (Essay); Cécile B. Evans (Diary)
description:
The catalogue of a 2020 group exhibition at HeK Basel on how digital technology reads emotion and how people form attachments to machines.

Twenty artists are presented, among them Antoine Catala, Heather Dewey-Hagborg, Justine Emard, Cécile B. Evans, Lucy McRae, Troika and Liam Young. Their work covers artificial intelligence, interactive installations, robotics, biometrics, video, VR and photography. Themes include humanoid robots in healthcare, sex robots and appliances that listen to conversations. Ariane Koek writes on feeling and post-truth. The neuroscientist António Damásio explains the biological role of feelings and how they might be built into robots. Cécile B. Evans contributes a diary on feelings and the interface. The show ran from 27 August to 15 November 2020.

The book is edited by the curators Sabine Himmelsbach and Angelique Spaninks and was published with MU Hybrid Art House in Eindhoven. Himmelsbach also edited Coding Care: Towards a Technology for Nature (Hatje Cantz, 2023).

title: Medium Hot: Images in the Age of Heat
description:
Essays by the artist and filmmaker Hito Steyerl on what images, art and technology become once machine learning runs through everyday life and the climate is breaking down.

Steyerl argues that artistic and technological practices cannot be divorced from economic and political conditions. She traces how machine learning has spread into every part of life, and sets out the damage done in the competition between technology companies, with AI-driven surveillance among her subjects. Verso published the hardback in June 2025 and a paperback in June 2026, both at 192 pages.

Steyerl is an artist and filmmaker whose work deals with the digital world, art and capitalism. Earlier books include I Will Survive (Spector Books) and This Is the Future (Prestel). Medium Hot extends that work to artificial intelligence.

The catalogue of MoMA's 2023 exhibition on video, which the museum describes as its first major publication on video art in nearly thirty years.

The book follows video from its debut as a consumer medium in the 1960s, through its spread across phones, screens, walls and streets. It draws on works from MoMA's collection and looks at artists who hoped video would build new networks of communication and public participation, and others who protested commercial and state control over information. Michelle Kuo and Stuart Comer edited the volume, with further texts by Erika Balsom and Tiffany Sia. The artists include Ant Farm, Dara Birnbaum, Black Audio Film Collective, Dan Graham, Nam June Paik, Martha Rosler, Martine Syms, Marlon Riggs and Videofreex.

title: Not Fully Human, Not Human at All
description:
The catalogue of a three-year curatorial project, initiated by Kadist, on dehumanization in Europe and what the project calls re-humanization.

The title comes from Donna Haraway's essay "Ecce Homo, Ain't (Ar'n't) I a Woman, and Inappropriate/d Others", which questions the universal claims of Enlightenment humanism. The book was published for exhibitions at Kunstverein in Hamburg (24 October 2020 to 7 February 2021) and Kadist, Paris (20 May to 11 July 2021). It collects contributions from artists, curators and theorists, including Saddie Choua, Daniela Ortiz, Lala Rašćić, Nora Sternfeld and Zairong Xiang. It is in English and German, with design by Charlotte Rohde. It was published by Archive Books with the Akademie der Künste der Welt, Cologne.

It is edited by Bettina Steinbrügge of Kunstverein in Hamburg and Émilie Villez of Kadist. Nataša Petrešin-Bachelez, who curated the project, is credited as managing editor with Nicholas Tammens. Kadist is a contemporary arts organization that runs residencies, exhibitions and publications.

title: Exquisite Errors: Diagnostic Manual of Codec Orders (DMCO-I)
contributors: Trudy Dehue (Foreword); Jos Jansen (Text editing); Sebastiaan Hanekroot (Lithography)
description:
A diagnostic manual for digital glitches, in which the Dutch artist Barry van der Rijt classifies codec errors the way psychiatry classifies mental disorders.

Over two years van der Rijt produced and catalogued more than 300 distorted images, each a codec order with its own entry. The classification follows the model of the DSM, with one reversal: every order is labelled positively rather than as a defect. The book has a foreword by Trudy Dehue, was designed by Rob van Hoesel and Carel Fransen, and runs to 288 pages in an Otastar softcover. The first edition was 500 copies.

Van der Rijt was diagnosed with ADHD about a decade before the book appeared, and the project treats his own diagnosis as a reason to look at deviation as something to describe rather than correct. The Eriskay Connection of Breda published it in 2015.

title: Affect Me: Social Media Images in Art
contributors: Lara Baladi (Artist); Irene Chabr (Artist); Lynn Hershman Leeson (Artist); Thomas Hirschhorn (Artist); Randa Maroufi (Artist); Rabih Mroué (Artist); Thomas Ruff (Artist); D. H. Saur (Artist)
description:
A catalogue on how artists use images taken from social media, and on how those images move people and carry emotion.

The book accompanies the exhibition at KAI 10 | Arthena Foundation in Düsseldorf, shown 11 November 2017 to 10 March 2018. It presents artists who work with social media imagery, often of political events, and treats that imagery as sitting between factual reporting and construction. Its premise is that such images help form communities and circulate emotional affects. The participating artists are Lara Baladi, Irene Chabr, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Thomas Hirschhorn, Randa Maroufi, Rabih Mroué, Thomas Ruff and D. H. Saur. Text is in German and English, in a thread-sewn hardcover designed by Krispin Heé and Studio Daniel Rother.

The editors, Julia Höner and Kerstin Schankweiler, curated the show. The project is associated with project B01 of the CRC 1171 Affective Societies research centre at Freie Universität Berlin. Spector Books published it in Leipzig in November 2017.

title: Handbook for Human Machines
description:
An artist's book by Maximilian Goldfarb that gathers visual research on how humans are extended and remade by machines.

The handbook holds two aspects of the visual research that formed Human Machine, a radio program Goldfarb produced for Wave Farm and broadcast from the FM station WGXC in New York's Hudson Valley. Together the book and the program accumulate, organize and represent developments for the extension and evolution of humans, tracing an evolving anatomy and shifting constructs of personhood. The book runs to 207 pages. Past episodes of the program are held in the Wave Farm transmission arts archive.

Goldfarb also publishes as Max Goldfarb. Publication Studio's Hudson studio published the book.

title: Die ungerahmte Welt / The Unframed World: Virtuelle Realität als künstlerisches Medium / Virtual Reality as Artistic Medium
editor: Sabine Himmelsbach, HeK (Haus der elektronischen Künste Basel)
description:
A bilingual survey of virtual reality as an artistic medium, issued by the Haus der elektronischen Künste Basel (HeK) in 2017.

The book presents artistic positions that use virtual reality technologies, among them Giulia Bowinkel and Friedemann Banz, Marc Lee, Rachel Rossin and Alfredo Salazar-Caro. The works take up themes such as physical perception and physical laws, societal structures, architecture and poetry. Essays from several research perspectives place the works in the wider development of VR in art. It has 96 pages and 63 colour illustrations, with parallel text in German and English.

The volume is edited by Sabine Himmelsbach for HeK Basel, the Haus der elektronischen Künste. Christoph Merian Verlag, Basel, published it in June 2017.
